from google.colab import userdata

client = MongoClient(userdata.get("MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING"))

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei03 / 26
Week 10 · crud04 / 26

Insert syntax: one document at a time

The pattern is collection.insert_one(document).

  • collection identifies where the document goes: our variable is demo.
  • document is a Python dictionary of field–value pairs.
  • insert_one() adds that one document to MongoDB.

Our first practice document will be:

{"_id": 1, "name": "Alice", "likes": 2}

The _id values 1, 2, and 3 let us select a specific practice record in the next steps.

Reference: PyMongo — insert documents

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei04 / 26
Week 10 · crud05 / 26

Insert three documents with a for loop

documents = [
    {"_id": 1, "name": "Alice", "likes": 2},
    {"_id": 2, "name": "Ben", "likes": 5},
    {"_id": 3, "name": "Cara", "likes": 1}
]

for document in documents:
    demo.insert_one(document)

for row in demo.find():
    print(row)

The loop calls insert_one() three times. You should see the three documents.

Run the insert cell once. Reusing the same _id values raises a duplicate-key error; inspect lab9.demo before repeating the exercise.

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei05 / 26
Week 10 · crud06 / 26

Update one document: change a value

The pattern is collection.update_one(filter, update).

demo.update_one(
    {"_id": 1},
    {"$set": {"likes": 7}}
)

print(demo.find_one({"_id": 1}))
Part Meaning
{"_id": 1} Select Alice's document.
{"$set": {"likes": 7}} Change its likes value from 2 to 7.

Reference: PyMongo — update documents

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei06 / 26
Week 10 · crud07 / 26

Update one document: add a new field

Use the same $set syntax for a field that does not exist yet.

demo.update_one(
    {"_id": 2},
    {"$set": {"topic": "data"}}
)

print(demo.find_one({"_id": 2}))

Ben's document now includes "topic": "data". Its name and likes remain in the document.

A new field was added to the existing document. The collection still has three documents. This is how we can store an additional analysis field later.

Reference: MongoDB — $set changes or adds a field

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei07 / 26
Week 10 · crud08 / 26

Delete one document and show what remains

The pattern is collection.delete_one(filter).

demo.delete_one({"_id": 3})

for row in demo.find():
    print(row)

Cara's document is deleted. The printed results should contain:

_id name likes topic
1 Alice 7 field not present
2 Ben 5 data

Reference: PyMongo — delete documents

Document-query example: English tweets

This is an extension of the Week 9 lecture's English-language filter, not a query contained in the supplied three-question file. Reuse your own saved equivalent when available.

result = client["lab8"]["tweet_collection"].find(
    {"tweet.lang": "en"},
    {"_id": 0, "tweet.text": 1,
     "tweet.public_metrics.like_count": 1}
).limit(10)

Filter: English tweets. Projection: text and likes. Limit: up to ten matching documents.

The returned documents still contain nested tweet fields. Next, read them into Python and display those fields as columns.

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei14 / 26
Week 10 · pandas15 / 26

First: list(result) reads the records

Run the document query on the previous slide, then:

records = list(result)
print(records[:1])

result is the PyMongo object that provides the query's returned documents. list(result) reads them into a Python list of dictionaries.

records[:1] previews the first returned document. For example, its structure can look like this:

[{"tweet": {"text": "A classroom example.",
            "public_metrics": {"like_count": 12}}}]

Fictional shape example, not a result to submit. The records variable contains your own returned data.

Use records in later cells. To read the query again, rerun the query cell first; reading result again after it has been consumed returns no more rows.

Reference: PyMongo: retrieve all documents as a list

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei15 / 26
Week 10 · pandas16 / 26

Then: json_normalize(records) makes columns

df = pd.json_normalize(records)
display(df)

pd is pandas. json_normalize() turns nested dictionaries into a flat table. It does not run a MongoDB query or change the stored documents.

Value inside a returned documentDataFrame column
tweet → texttweet.text
tweet → public_metrics → like_counttweet.public_metrics.like_count

The field names supply the column names automatically. You do not have to know the tweet text, likes, or hashtag values in advance.

For the already-flat Q1 record {"tweet_count": 200}, pd.DataFrame(records) is enough. Use json_normalize when the result contains nested fields.

The number above illustrates the supplied file's earlier Q1 answer, not a live result. Reference: pandas json_normalize

Optional: make the table easier to read

OPTIONAL FORMATTING The previous slide has already loaded the data. You can keep that DataFrame and its original field names.

df = df.reindex(columns=[
    "tweet.text", "tweet.public_metrics.like_count"
])
df.columns = ["Tweet text", "Likes"]

pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", None)
display(df)
  • reindex(columns=...) selects and orders the two columns; it does not load the query again.
  • df.columns = ... replaces their headings, in that order.
  • display.max_colwidth = None lets the table show the full text.

Check first: inspect df.columns. A misspelled or absent name passed to reindex produces missing values, not a new MongoDB query. This formatting is optional; readable output is the goal.

Reference: pandas reindex

Aggregation example: hashtag counts

Reuse your saved hashtag query when you have one, or develop it with MongoDB AI. This example comes from the Week 9 lecture; it is not present in the supplied Q1–Q3 file.

result = client["lab8"]["tweet_collection"].aggregate([
    {"$unwind": {"path": "$tweet.entities.hashtags"}},
    {"$sortByCount": "$tweet.entities.hashtags.tag"},
    {"$limit": 10}
])

MongoDB returns one record per hashtag: _id contains the tag and count contains its number of occurrences.

This uses the Week 9 counting rule with a limit of 10. Stored spelling and case stay unchanged: Election and election remain separate.

References: Week 9 hashtag example · MongoDB $sortByCount

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei19 / 26
Week 10 · pandas20 / 26

Read the counts: check the output field names

Inspect the query output first. This $sortByCount pipeline returns _id (the tag) and count (its occurrences). 

records = list(result)
df = pd.DataFrame(records, columns=["_id", "count"])
df.columns = ["Hashtag", "Occurrences"]
display(df)
Returned fieldMeaningHeading chosen here
_idHashtag valueHashtag
countNumber of occurrencesOccurrences

The names are not guessed. columns=["_id", "count"] selects known fields in a known order and keeps those headings even for an empty result. The next line renames them for display and plotting.

Optional: can pandas infer the column names?

Yes. With non-empty dictionary records, pd.DataFrame(records) uses their keys as column names. You can keep _id and count without renaming them, provided the later plot uses those same names. With an empty list, pandas has no keys from which to infer names.

For a different AI-generated pipeline, inspect records[:1] or display its DataFrame and check df.columns. Use the actual output fields, not names copied blindly from this example.

Now df holds hashtag counts, not English tweets. The next chart uses this new table; MongoDB data is unchanged.

References: MongoDB $sortByCount · pandas DataFrame

IA 340 · Week 10 · Dr. Xuebin Wei20 / 26
Week 10 · pandas21 / 26

Plot the aggregation result

if df.empty:
    print("No hashtags found: 0 occurrences.")
else:
    ax = df.plot.barh(
        x="Hashtag", y="Occurrences", legend=False,
        figsize=(8, 4)
    )
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.set(title="Top hashtags in my collected tweets",
           xlabel="Occurrences", ylabel="Hashtag")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

x names the label column; y names the numeric column. The horizontal bars compare the counts already in df.
